paper_title: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at https://github.com/Shengxiang-Lin/PGPO.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have leveraged their rich semantic understanding to provide high-quality embeddings for item side information (Wu et al., 2024). This approach effectively alleviates data sparsity and cold-start issues in recommendation. However, these embeddings may leak sensitive user information (Song *Corresponding Authors. Figure 1: Motivation for relational-fidelity obfuscation in protecting item side information for LLM-enhanced recommendation. and Raghunathan, 2020; Wang et al., 2025). Embedding inversion attacks can reconstruct the original text from public embeddings with high accuracy, and the risk increases when data is sent to uncontrolled third-party LLM APIs (Tsai et al., 2026). Faced with this input-side threat, existing defenses struggle. Post-hoc recommendation protections such as differential privacy in recommender systems (Dwork et al., 2006; Müllner et al., 2023) and federated learning for recommendation (McMahan et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2021) assume trustworthy collector and can hardly prevent leakage once data leaves the device. Traditional synonym-substitution obfuscation stays at the word level (Jin et al., 2020), treating items as isolated tokens and easily shattering semantics, thereby destroying semantic relationships between items anchored by side information. To simultaneously protect privacy and maintain utility, input-side protection should achieve two semantic-level goals. The first goal is to induce sufficient semantic shift so that embedding inversion attacks cannot exploit the invertible mapping between embeddings and their source texts (Morris et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). If obfuscated embeddings remain too close to the original, attackers can still approximate the text. Therefore, embeddings must move away from the original to break this invertible connection. The second goal is to preserve local semantic neighborhood structure that connect cold and popular items through shared attributes (Vasile et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023). Maintaining these relative relationships preserves the semantic skeleton needed for recommendation without requiring global semantic fidelity. Traditional discrete token-level substitution cannot finely control the magnitude or direction of changes in continuous embedding space. Such perturbations disrupt local semantic relations and tightly couple deviation strength with order preservation, making joint optimization impossible. The discretecontinuousdiscrete pipeline of LLM allows fine-grained manipulation of embeddings before decoding (Naparstek, 2026; Zhang et al., 2023), generating new words while decoupling deviation strength from relational structure. However, recent LLM-based text privacy methods, e.g., EmojiPrompt (Lin et al., 2025), LLMAnonymization (Staab et al., 2025), and IncogniText (Frikha et al., 2025), all follow semantic fidelity, hiding private attributes while preserving literal meaning. This misaligns with recommender systems, which need relational fidelity, i.e., preserving the relative semantic skeleton across items rather than literal text. Under relational fidelity, obfuscated content can be arbitrary as long as usable item similarity structure persists, turning the task from constrained masking into active topology reconstruction. LLMs naturally suit this, yet existing methods were never designed for it. To realize relational fidelity, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO) framework with three sequential stages: prototype-aware graph construction, prototype variant exploration, and anchor-oriented graph expansion. We first identify high-influence prototypes and build static semantic neighbor graph to capture their structural impact. The LLM then explores suitable obfuscated variants for these prototypes, which serve as stable structural anchors. Finally, the framework propagates these anchored mappings through the static graph to cover the remaining vocabulary. This process is optimized using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) with three complementary rewards: i) individual dissimilarity maximizes embedding distance to enforce semantic shift, ii) structural consistency preserves local similarity order to maintain the semantic distribution necessary for recommendation, and iii) semantic anchoring constrains generation within category-specific semantic manifolds to prevent degenerate shortcuts. By jointly optimizing these rewards, the framework balances privacy and utility, protecting sensitive information while preserving the relative semantic structure crucial for recommendation. Our contributions are as follows: We formulate input-side obfuscation for LLMenhanced recommendation as topologypreserving privacy problem, introducing relational fidelity to defend against embedding inversion while preserving relative item semantics. We propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation framework that scales topologyaware obfuscation from high-influence prototype words to the full vocabulary. We design three GRPO rewards, i.e., individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint, to jointly enforce semantic shift and preserve item relations. Under aligned CosSim, experiments on two benchmarks show that our method achieves the highest recommendation utility at comparable defense strength.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: LLM-Enhanced Recommender Systems. Large language models (LLMs) have reshaped recommender systems, either as semantic enhancers enriching item metadata, user profiles, and interaction graphs (Wu et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2024), or as direct recommenders via language modeling, prompting, instruction tuning, or parameterefficient fine-tuning, covering frameworks like P5 (Geng et al., 2022), M6-Rec (Cui et al., 2022), TALLRec (Bao et al., 2023), LLaRA (Liao et al., 2024) and ReLLa (Lin et al., 2024), and ranking or explanation models (Dai et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b). However, encoding side information and interactions into continuous embeddings raises privacy concerns. User clicks can be inferred from exposure (Xin et al., 2023), and LLM recommenders are vulnerable to inversion attacks (Wang et al., 2025), underscoring the need for input-level privacy protection (Luo et al., 2024). Embedding Inversion Attacks. Embedding inversion attacks aim to reconstruct original text or sensitive attributes from exposed embeddings, posing significant privacy risks in NLP. Early studies demonstrated that embedding models leak rich semantic information (Song and Raghunathan, 2020; Fredrikson et al., 2015). Subsequent work further recovered full sentences using generative decoders (Li et al., 2023a) and inverted dense embeddings with high fidelity through iterative optimization and beam search (Morris et al., 2023). Recent attacks further expose practical vulnerabilities under cross-model (Huang et al., 2024), blackbox (Chen et al., 2025), multilingual (Chen et al., 2024), and zero-shot settings (Zhang et al., 2025), motivating input-side protection for recommendation embeddings. Text Obfuscation Defenses. Text obfuscation protects privacy by perturbing raw text while preserving downstream utility. Existing approaches include wordor character-level substitution and adversarial perturbation (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Jia and Liang, 2017), homograph or typo-based replacement, and context-aware embedding perturbation (Zhou et al., 2023), as well as differential privacy-based sanitization such as SanText/SanText+ (Yue et al., 2021) and local DP token mapping (Feyisetan et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2021; Mai et al., 2023). Other methods exploit controlled paraphrasing, masking, or hybrid perturbations to hide sensitive attributes. Recent work explores LLM-based privacy protection, including prompt obfuscation (Lin et al., 2025), LLM-based anonymization (Staab et al., 2025), conditional attribute randomization (Frikha et al., 2025), utilityaware rewriting (Yang et al., 2025b), and privacypreserving LLM inference (Tong et al., 2025b). However, these studies mostly target general NLP text, user-generated content, or LLM prompts, leaving privacy-preserving obfuscation for item-side textual metadata in recommender systems largely underexplored.

(a) Normalized variant quality metric changes relative to the full model. 5.3 Ablation Study We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the contribution of each component, where we set variants as: (1) w/o GRPO, directly generating outputs with the LLM; (2) w/o context, removing context examples and generating each word independently; (3) w/o dissimilarity, removing the individual dissimilarity reward; (4) w/o structural, removing the structural consistency reward; and (5) w/o constraint, removing the semantic constraint reward. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we addressed input-level privacy for LLM-enhanced recommender systems. By shifting from semantic fidelity to relational fidelity, we proposed PGPO, prototype-guided progressive obfuscation framework. Both theoretical analysis and experiments show that PGPO achieves stronger privacyutility trade-off than baselines while preserving recommendation utility. Future work may extend the framework to other modalities and decentralized deployment.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our framework currently treats side-information words with unified obfuscation strategy, without explicitly assigning higher protection priority to more sensitive or rare words over generic ones. Future work may incorporate sensitivityaware weighting to better allocate privacy budgets across words. Additionally, PGPO introduces extra computational cost due to LLM-based variant generation, which may be mitigated in future work through offline caching, batch generation, lightweight policy distillation, or retrieval-based reuse of high-quality obfuscation mappings. Moreover, our current study focuses primarily on textual side information, leaving the extension of relational fidelity to multimodal inputs such as images, audio, video, and knowledge graphs for future work. risk is that the obfuscation could be misused to bypass content moderation by replacing prohibited items with innocuous expressions.

The resulting retained categories and keyword counts are reported in Table 6. B.3 Baselines We compare our method with the following baselines: None: Item embeddings constructed without using side information, serving as the lower bound. Description: Raw side information, serving as the utility upper bound. InferDPT: differentially private text perturbation method that injects Laplacian noise during text encoding (Tong et al., 2025b), used directly without LLM processing. Text2Text: sequence-to-sequence text obfuscation method that perturbs embeddings under local differential privacy and decodes them back (Feyisetan et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2021). SanText+: An improved text obfuscation method that optimizes substitution word selection to enhance obfuscation quality (Yue et al., 2021). TextObfuscator (TOF): rule-based text obfuscation tool that replaces sensitive words for privacy protection (Zhou et al., 2023). Embedding Inversion Attack. We adopt the Vec2Text embedding inversion attack (Morris et al., 2023) to recover sensitive category labels from item embeddings. The attack training data does not overlap with the items used in the main recommendation experiments. For MovieLens-1M, we sample 80,000 movie tags from MovieLens25M3 and MovieLens-32M4. For Amazon-Book, we sample 100,000 disjoint items. Embeddings are generated using the same pipeline as in the main experiments. Since different obfuscation methods induce different degrees of semantic displacement, directly comparing attack success rates can be misleading. For fair evaluation, we tune the hyperparameters of each method, such as dissimilarity reward and DP noise, so that the average cosine similarity between original and obfuscated embeddings is aligned. All inversion attacks are evaluated under this aligned CosSim setting. Maximum-likelihood Inversion Attack. We consider strong white-box attacker with access to the optimized conversion model, original vocabulary, static semantic graph, retrieval function ϕ, and generation prompt. The attacker observes the released variant z, but not the cached history or the realized generation trajectory Γ. For each observed variant, we construct candidate set containing the ground-truth source word and 50 sampled negatives. For each candidate xi C, the attacker replays the generation prompt with = and computes the teacher-forced likelihood of z. B.5 Feature Processing Pipeline All original and obfuscated texts are encoded into 768-dimensional embeddings using BERT-baseuncased. For traditional recommendation models, PCA is applied to reduce the dimension to 128. For multimodal and LLM-based models, the full 768-dimensional embeddings are retained and integrated through learnable projection layers. B.6 Training Configuration For both datasets, the prototype word count is set to 5000, the cache size is set to 2000, the reward weights are (λdis, λstr, λcon) = (1, 2, 1), and the 3https://grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/25m/ 4https://grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/32m/ warm-up length is Twarmup = 2 (cid:24) CPrototype batch_size (cid:25) . After sufficient high-quality anchors are cached, the structural consistency reward is restored to its default weight. All ablation and parameter sensitivity experiments are conducted on MovieLens-1M. For ablation studies, we use the same hyperparameter settings as the MovieLens-1M main experiment unless otherwise specified. For parameter sensitivity analysis, we vary one factor at time while keeping the others fixed. In cache size sensitivity, we set (λdis, λstr, λcon) = (1, 1, 1) and vary the cache size in {0, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000}. In prototype word count sensitivity, we use (λdis, λstr, λcon) = (1, 2, 1) and vary the prototype word count in {1250, 2500, 5000, 7500, 10000}. In reward weight sensitivity, we fix the cache size to 2000 and start from (λdis, λstr, λcon) = (1, 1, 1). We then vary λdis, λstr, and λcon individually, with each weight taking values from {1, 2, 3}. The batch size is set to 2, and all PGPO training and generation experiments are conducted on single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU with 24GB memory. B.7 Evaluation Metrics We evaluate our method from three perspectives: obfuscated variants quality, recommendation performance, and embedding inversion defense B.7.1 Obfuscated Variants Quality We evaluate generation quality at both the word and context levels. For word-level evaluation, we encode original words and generated variants with BERT-baseuncased embeddings. We report Distinct-1 (Li et al., 2016) to measure token-level diversity, and use Spearman correlation to evaluate whether the local semantic structure is preserved after transformation. In addition, we define Valid, Spearman and LR for our task. For each original word, we retrieve its top-k nearest neighbors within the same category in the original BERT embedding space, and compare the similarity rankings before and after transformation using Spearman rank correlation (Spearman, 1961). We average the correlation over all valid samples: Spearman = 1 N (cid:88) i=1 ρi, (48) where ρi denotes the rank correlation for the i-th sample. higher value indicates better preservation of the local neighborhood structure. We report Distinct-2 (Li et al., 2016) to measure contextual diversity. We use Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025a) to compute KL divergence (Nalewajski, 2011) and NLL (Bengio et al., 2003), where KL measures the average divergence between token probability distributions of original and transformed contexts, and NLL (from LM cross-entropy loss) evaluates the fluency of the transformed contexts. As reported in Table 9 and Fig. 10, increasing its weight improves Spearman correlation, confirming that this reward helps preserve local semantic topology. Meanwhile, D-1 and D-2 increase slightly, and NLL rises only moderately, suggesting that the model can strengthen relational consistency without severely sacrificing diversity or fluency. Fig. 10c shows that the semantic constraint reward affects both global layout and local sample positions. As shown in Table 9 and Fig. 10, increasing its weight encourages generated variants to stay closer to the category-specific semantic manifold, improving semantic validity and preventing degenerate outputs. However, overly strong semantic constraints make the variants closer to the original words, as reflected by higher CosSim and reduced diversity.
